summary: If you release games commercially, treat every game players could spend their hours on, new or old, as your competition, and let gratitude for that abundance fuel your work.
takeaways: You compete for players' hours against every game ever made
Subscription services pit new releases against back catalogs
Player abundance exists because creators braved the competition
Making games deepens your understanding of why games are fun

principles.principle: Benchmark your game against past classics, not only new releases
principles.why: Games take many hours to play, so every developer competes for player time, and subscription services make competition with past titles unavoidable.
principles.how: Before committing to a commercial project, list the old and new games your target player could play instead, and define why they would choose yours.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming your game will find players just because you think it is fun.
principles.example: Subscription services placing older catalog titles beside new releases.
principles.quote: Remember, you're not only competing against the latest titles, but those created in the past as well.

principles.principle: Keep creating games to deepen your understanding of why games are fun
principles.why: Others will keep creating if you quit, so stay because you want to; Sakurai says making games himself deepened his understanding of why games are fun.
principles.how: Treat each project, even a hobby one, as study of what makes games fun, and remember how much labor sits behind every game you play.
principles.quote: By taking the leap into the field of game creation myself, I’ve gained a deeper understanding and awareness of why games are fun.

summary: Every now and then, play a game completely blind, with no trailers, spoilers, strategy guides or Let's Plays, because it lets you feel more and it is the best way to study someone else's work.
takeaways: Occasionally play games completely blind, avoiding all spoilers
Skip trailers, guides and Let's Plays until finished
Form your own impressions before reading others' opinions
Blind play is the best way to study others' work

principles.principle: Study others' games by playing them blind, without spoilers or guides
principles.why: Without preconceptions your impressions are your own, you feel more and you experience every surprise; Sakurai calls this the best way to study someone else's work.
principles.how: Avoid trailers, strategy sites and Let's Plays until you finish, and open a guide only as a last resort when truly stuck.
principles.anti_pattern: Watching Let's Plays or reading guides before forming your own impressions.
principles.quote: In terms of studying someone else's work, there's no better way to do it than this.

principles.principle: Form your own verdict before looking up what others think
principles.why: Sakurai wants his impressions to be his alone, without anything else coloring his opinion.
principles.how: Finish the game and settle your own impressions first, then read reviews and community discussion.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting buzz or others' takes shape your view before you have played.
principles.quote: If you want to know what other people think, wait until you're done to look into it.

summary: Don't take the score for granted: give it a meaningful unit of measurement, such as an age, money or a power rating, and present each increase so that earning it feels great.
takeaways: Never take the score for granted; design its presentation
Express scores in a meaningful unit of measurement
Concrete units like money make the experience feel real
Count score increases up point by point

principles.principle: Express scores in a meaningful unit instead of bare points
principles.why: Having something to strive for is what makes games fun; recasting the number as an age, money or power changes the game's meaning and makes the experience feel more real.
principles.how: Pick a unit that fits your game's fantasy, such as Brain Age, Crash Dollars or Global Smash Power, and choose its direction (lower is better for an age).
principles.anti_pattern: Dropping in a plain score counter without thinking about how it is presented.
principles.example: Brain Age presents your score as your brain's age; Burnout's Crash Mode scores in Crash Dollars.
principles.quote: The trick is that each variation is still based on a unit of measurement.

principles.principle: Count score gains up point by point so they feel better
principles.why: Even a conventional score deserves careful presentation, and showing the increase step by step can make that part of the design feel even better.
principles.how: Animate each score award as a running tally instead of snapping the total straight to its new value.
principles.quote: I'd also consider things like showing the score increase point-by-point to potentially make that aspect of the game's design feel even better.

summary: Give effects enough density to match the world's scale: a large flame needs many loops or small, detailed particles, or it will read as a candle.
takeaways: Effects must match the world's sense of scale
Big flames lacking density look like candles
Add loops or smaller, detailed particles for density
Effects move constantly; make them quick and fierce, not detailed

principles.principle: Give large effects enough density to read at the right scale
principles.why: A flame as big as a character but lacking density reads as a candle or torch, which Sakurai calls an extremely common trap.
principles.how: Increase the number of flame loops or use smaller, more detailed particles, and give effect artists a reference image of the density you want.
principles.anti_pattern: Big flames built from a few large shapes.
principles.example: Pyra's sword flames looked candle-like until Sakurai supplied a density reference.
principles.quote: As a general rule for creating effects, keep the size of the world in mind and try to preserve the proper sense of scale.

principles.principle: Spend effect budget on quick, fierce motion rather than fine detail
principles.why: Chasing density eats into texture memory, but effects are constantly in motion, so they don't need to be overly detailed.
principles.how: Keep effect textures modest and put iteration time into speed and motion so the effect looks quick and fierce.
principles.anti_pattern: Over-detailing effects until they eat up texture memory.
principles.example: Texture limits kept Pyra's final sword swing from getting closer to the target density.
principles.quote: The key is making them look quick and fierce.

summary: Decide on purpose how much your competitive game should even out skill: casual games need catch-up systems so everyone gets turns winning, while a game meant to reflect skill should limit leveling to chaotic elements and optional settings.
takeaways: Casual games need catch-up systems so everyone wins sometimes
Skill-focused games shouldn't buff trailing players' stats
Route catch-up through chaos: items, stages, comeback meters
Human adjustments are the most effective handicap

principles.principle: Give casual competitive games catch-up mechanics so wins rotate
principles.why: Games where the most skilled player wins every time aren't fun, and in an average household different people should take turns winning.
principles.how: Give trailing players speed boosts or stronger items, as Mario Kart does, and accept that the leader can be dethroned.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting the most skilled player win every match in a casual game.
principles.example: Mario Kart's speed boosts and items for trailing players.
principles.quote: Games where the person with the most skill keeps winning every single time just aren't fun.

principles.principle: In skill-driven games, level the field through chaos, not stat buffs
principles.why: Sakurai wanted Smash results to reflect skill, so trailing players get no attack or knockback help, while chaotic items, stages and Final Smashes still shake up outcomes.
principles.how: Make power-ups harder for the leader to obtain and charge comeback meters faster for losing players, leaving core stats untouched.
principles.anti_pattern: Raising attack power or reducing knockback for players who are behind.
principles.example: Smash Bros.: the leader has a harder time getting a Smash Ball, and the Final Smash Meter charges faster for losing players.
principles.quote: In other words, chaotic, anything-goes content like Final Smashes, items, stages, and even Final Smash Meters are a great fit for a party game, I’d say.

principles.principle: Design local multiplayer to tolerate quirks players can house-rule
principles.why: At home, players can talk out their differences, and banning a cheap move becomes part of the fun or a memory, so a bit of weirdness is OK.
principles.how: When designing mainly for local play, accept minor exploits players can ban themselves, and offer an optional automatic handicap setting.
principles.example: Sakurai's Smash Bros. Brawl proposal noted the game targets home play and is in some ways unsuited to online play.
principles.quote: So it's OK if there's a bit of weirdness there.

summary: A game with little push-and-pull can still hook players if it simulates real-world work, runs a work-earn-upgrade loop and keeps the ending out of sight.
takeaways: Fun can exist without push-and-pull or risk
Base work games on real-world tasks players can imagine
Design the work-earn-upgrade loop first
Hide the ending far away if there isn't one

principles.principle: Build a work-earn-upgrade loop first in task-based games
principles.why: Working, earning money and then buying tools and skills that make the work easier gives work games their staying power; Sakurai calls it the first element to consider.
principles.how: Make each job pay out currency that buys tools or skills which make the next job easier to finish.
principles.anti_pattern: A work simulation with no profit or upgrade loop.
principles.example: Car Mechanic Simulator, House Flipper and PowerWash Simulator all let you profit from the work.
principles.quote: Without this loop, a game about work wouldn't have nearly as much staying power.

principles.principle: Ground task games in real-world work so imagination fills gaps
principles.why: With a real-world subject the player's mind fills in extra information, and striving toward the desired outcome keeps players doing the work.
principles.how: Pick a recognizable job such as repair, renovation or cleaning, make the desired end result clear, and set the mood so players role-play the job.
principles.example: House Flipper: cleaning up a room feels great, and a house can start to feel like your own home.

principles.principle: If there's no ending, place the goal beyond the player's sight
principles.why: Real-world tasks and profit create a synergy that keeps players from stopping, and when there is no clear ending a far-off goal keeps them going.
principles.how: Use exponential growth or very distant milestones, as Cookie Clicker does, so players never see the finish line.
principles.example: Cookie Clicker's exponentially growing cookie production.
principles.quote: If your game lacks a clear ending, you might as well place it so far away that players can't even see where they're heading.

summary: Mix ambient sounds at the lowest priority so they never mask important effects, but don't cut them, because quiet, fairly realistic ambience is what makes the game world feel real.
takeaways: Ambient sounds take the lowest mix priority
Never let ambience mask important sound effects
Dead silence kills atmosphere; always layer ambience
Use realistic ambience even in cartoony games

principles.principle: Mix ambient sounds lowest so key sound effects stay audible
principles.why: Ambient sounds are the least important, so if they stand out, players can't hear the sound effects that really matter.
principles.how: Give ambience the lowest priority and volume in your mix, and verify that no gameplay-critical effect is ever masked.
principles.anti_pattern: Ambience loud or busy enough to bury important effects.
principles.example: Smash Bros. stages contain many ambient sounds that are hard to hear at normal volume.
principles.quote: Hence, if they stand out too much, you won't be able to hear the sound effects that really matter— and that's a problem.

principles.principle: Never leave dead silence; layer subtle ambience for immersion
principles.why: Silence when the player stops kills the atmosphere, players with good speakers will notice the ambience, and immersion matters most in first-person or over-the-shoulder views.
principles.how: Stop in each area and listen, and add quiet environmental layers wherever you hear nothing, especially in first-person or over-the-shoulder games.
principles.anti_pattern: Dead silence whenever the action pauses.
principles.quote: Additionally, if you stop playing for a second and hear nothing but dead silence, there'll be no sense of atmosphere.

principles.principle: Use realistic recordings for ambience, exaggerated sounds for actions
principles.why: Unlike other sound effects, which generally need exaggeration, fairly realistic audio works well for ambience, even in cartoony games.
principles.how: Use realistic environmental recordings for ambience and layer them under your stylized gameplay effects.
principles.quote: As opposed to other sound effects which generally need to be more exaggerated, relatively realistic audio works great for ambient sounds.

summary: A game world is a massless mirage, so control every asset's texture, response to light, weight, use and placement, along with invisible things like airflow, until the world feels real.
takeaways: Game worlds are massless mirages; expression makes them feel real
Control texture, light, weight, use and placement of assets
Presentation and arrangement decide whether objects feel real
Simulate invisible forces like wind and explosion gusts

principles.principle: Design props for texture, light, weight, use and placement, not just shape
principles.why: Game objects have no physical presence, and a regular table and a miniature one share the same shape, so only presentation and arrangement make a world feel real.
principles.how: For each asset, specify how it catches light, how heavy it should feel, what it is used for and where it sits, then review it in the scene.
principles.anti_pattern: Making something that merely looks like a table.
principles.example: A table with things on it, compared with a miniature table of the same shape.
principles.quote: Take a look at the big picture, and try to make the imaginary feel real.

principles.principle: Simulate invisible forces like airflow to sell physical presence
principles.why: Airflow is an easy oversight because we normally can't see it, yet visuals, audio, programming and parameters together create the sense of authenticity.
principles.how: Add environmental wind that makes loose objects flutter, and small gusts of wind around explosions.
principles.anti_pattern: Forgetting invisible forces such as wind.
principles.example: Smash Bros.: environmental wind makes things flutter, with slight gusts near explosions.
principles.quote: An easy oversight to make here is in regards to airflow.

summary: Start each character from a neutral, workable baseline, then push their parameters and unique mechanics far enough that their identity fits in a word or two, and budget the programming that takes.
takeaways: Start neutral, then deviate boldly for each character
Describe each character's identity in a word or two
Unique mechanics require dedicated programming; budget for it
Emphasize parameter differences; fix issues during production

principles.principle: Start from a neutral baseline, then push each character far from it
principles.why: Unusable eccentricity is pointless, but characters that are basically the same are no fun; maximizing deviation from a workable neutral creates gameplay possibilities and strategy.
principles.how: Define a neutral character for your rules, exaggerate specific parameters for each character, and iron out problems as production continues.
principles.anti_pattern: Small, timid parameter changes, or a ship that shoots everywhere except forward.
principles.example: Each Smash Bros. Ultimate DLC fighter has a unique system, from the Rebellion Gauge to magic cycling.
principles.quote: Numbers are a big part of what brings characters to life! Don't just make small changes, but emphasize the differences

principles.principle: Make each character describable in a word or two
principles.why: Distinct traits introduce strategy and make characters memorable, the way Gordo sticks in players' memory differently from other enemies.
principles.how: Write a one- or two-word identity for every character or enemy, and if you can't, push its traits further.
principles.example: Gordo: invincible, never attacks, no movement pattern.
principles.quote: In my view, characters should be made unique enough that you can describe their distinctive traits in just a word or two.

principles.principle: Give enemies traits that gain meaning from their placement
principles.why: Gordo alone would be an uninteresting enemy, but positioned near other enemies it gains significance in a number of ways.
principles.how: Design some enemies as pure obstacles (invincible, harmless, static) and place them to shape how players handle the enemies around them.
principles.example: Kirby series: Gordo placed near other enemies.
principles.quote: If you just drop one into the game, it would make for a completely uninteresting enemy.

principles.principle: Budget programming for each character's one-of-a-kind mechanic
principles.why: For a character to do something no one else can, there has to be specific programming supporting it, and that cost can't be avoided.
principles.how: Schedule engineering time per character for its unique system, such as a gauge, resource, stance switch or special input.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate DLC: Persona, MP and Commands, Heroes' Relics, the double ARMS system, block building and more.
principles.quote: For a character to do something no one else can, there needs to be specific programming to support that.

summary: When you demo your game, plan your play so it shows as much of the content as possible in close matches, and imagine presenting your work even if you never will, because doing so organizes your thinking.
takeaways: Showing a game directly is the most effective presentation
Demo every special move and the super move
Keep demo matches relatively close
Imagining a presentation organizes your thoughts and reveals insights

principles.principle: Plan demos to show every key feature in close matches
principles.why: Showing a game directly is probably the most effective form of presentation, so the goal is to capture as much quality footage as possible.
principles.how: Make a checklist of all special moves, the super move and as many regular moves as possible, and keep matches relatively close.
principles.anti_pattern: Demoing without understanding the game's content.
principles.example: Mr. Sakurai Presents: Sakurai played each DLC fighter himself, using all of its special moves and its Final Smash.
principles.quote: To put it simply, I'm always trying to get as much quality footage as I can.

principles.principle: Imagine presenting your work to customers to uncover insights
principles.why: Thinking up a presentation helps you organize your own thoughts (the teacher becomes the student), and picturing reactions can reveal new insights.
principles.how: Even if you will never present it, mentally walk through showing your game and note how players and customers would react.
principles.quote: Oh, and did you know that thinking up a presentation can help you organize your own thoughts?

summary: Run bug testing as a dedicated, ticket-driven system (latest daily build, systematic coverage, severity classes, routing to whoever can fix it, tickets kept as resolved), because every fix can create a new bug.
takeaways: Use dedicated bug testers, not programmers, for testing
Everyone tests the latest daily build
Track reproducible bugs as severity-classed tickets routed to owners
Keep fixed tickets resolved, never discarded
Every fix risks new bugs; find and fix fast

principles.principle: Test only on the latest daily build, and require reproduction steps
principles.why: Bugs found on the wrong version aren't helpful and can cause problems, and a reproducible ticket can be tracked and assigned so nothing is overlooked.
principles.how: Make the latest daily build mandatory for testers, and file each bug as an online ticket only once it can be reproduced.
principles.anti_pattern: Accepting bug reports from outdated builds.
principles.quote: To start, as a fundamental rule, we have to make sure that everyone is using the latest daily build of the game.

principles.principle: Classify bugs by severity and route each to the discipline that owns it
principles.why: Class S (hangs, save corruption) and Class A (progression blockers) come first, and programmers aren't always the right fixers: artists fix characters and animators fix animations.
principles.how: Have a manager tag each ticket S, A or lower (lower ones may be waived), assign it to the right subteam or person, and rebalance anyone with too many tickets.
principles.anti_pattern: Sending every bug to programmers by default.
principles.quote: Programmers aren't always the right people to fix bugs, after all.

principles.principle: Verify fixes across configurations and keep tickets as resolved
principles.why: Every fix risks introducing new bugs and old bugs can come back, so confirmed fixes stay on record instead of being discarded.
principles.how: Return each fixed ticket to its tester to confirm in several configurations, set it to resolved, and cross-reference or merge related tickets.
principles.anti_pattern: Deleting tickets once they are fixed.
principles.quote: However, the trickiest thing about bugs is that whenever you resolve one, you run the risk of introducing new bugs.

principles.principle: Automate overnight CPU matches to hunt bugs in combinatorial games
principles.why: In games with near-limitless combinations, or open worlds where players can go almost anywhere, human testing alone is far too cumbersome.
principles.how: Run CPU-vs-CPU battles overnight to surface bugs, and near the end of the project run worldwide playtests that pass save data between regions.
principles.example: Smash Bros. ran CPU battles all night; testers in Japan, North America and Europe passed save data back and forth.
principles.quote: With Smash Bros., we would occasionally run CPU battles all night long to find bugs.

summary: A history episode: 1986 produced an unusual number of lasting franchises because new storage capacity, fierce competition and fast growth drew people to games, and today's developers build on the paths those predecessors carved.
takeaways: 1986 launched many franchises that later appeared in Smash
Capacity jumps (Disk System, megabit ROMs) expanded what games could do
Rapid hardware and software progress drew people to games
Secrets delighted players but were tough on the uninformed
Build on predecessors' path, then carve your own

principles.principle: Study formative eras of games, then carve a new path
principles.why: The path today's creators walk was carved by their predecessors, and knowing it is the basis for creating a new path of your own.
principles.how: Play landmark titles from eras like 1986 (many are playable today) and note which conventions began there before designing your own.
principles.example: 1986: the Famicom Disk System and megabit ROMs expanded game capacity.
principles.quote: And now, we have to do our best to create a new path of our own.

principles.principle: Use hidden secrets for discovery, but don't punish uninformed players
principles.why: Hidden characters and secret codes heightened the surprise and joy of discovering the unknown, but it must have been tough for players who weren't in the know.
principles.how: Add secrets as bonuses, and make sure players can enjoy and finish the game without insider knowledge.
principles.example: Hidden characters and secret codes popular in Japan around 1986.
principles.quote: Though it must have been tough if you weren't in the know.

summary: Angle the fingers in a diagonal grip on anything swung with the forearm so it looks natural, and spend finger bones and processing only where they matter.
takeaways: Use a diagonal grip for objects swung with the forearm
Perpendicular grips make characters look like action figures
Fingers are the first thing cut under processing load
Swap pre-made finger patterns instead of full articulation

principles.principle: Pose swung objects in a diagonal grip, not perpendicular to fingers
principles.why: A perpendicular grip suits simply holding something, but swinging with the forearm uses a diagonal grip, and a perpendicular one makes characters look like action figures.
principles.how: Review every weapon or tool hold, and angle the fingers and the object diagonally for anything that gets swung.
principles.anti_pattern: Rigid perpendicular grips on swung weapons.
principles.quote: if you're going to swing it along with your forearm, you use a diagonal grip.

principles.principle: Cut finger articulation where processing is tight; spend it where it matters
principles.why: Fingers are very complex for their size, and giving structure to every finger on a busy screen and calculating its movement costs heavily.
principles.how: Lock finger joints so they only appear movable, swap in pre-made finger patterns when needed, and move the saved processing to more important parts.
principles.anti_pattern: Fully simulating every finger on screens crowded with characters.
principles.quote: Depending on the hardware and your goals, you'll constantly need to consider cutting where you can and diverting processing to the parts that matter.

summary: Let players get through text and dialogue at their own, usually fast, pace, with line-by-line skipping in cutscenes or voiced lines they can hear while playing, because modern players want to enjoy as much as possible in as little time as possible.
takeaways: Players read fast; let them zip through text
Offer line-by-line skipping in voiced cutscenes
Let players hear dialogue while they keep playing
Modern audiences want maximum enjoyment in minimum time

principles.principle: Let players speed through text and skip dialogue line by line
principles.why: People read quickly and zipping through text feels good, and everyone wants to enjoy as much as possible in as little time, as video playback-speed settings show.
principles.how: Let a button press complete and advance text immediately, and in cutscenes add a skip that jumps to the start of the next line.
principles.anti_pattern: Forcing everyone through text and scenes at one slow pace.
principles.example: Some games let you skip dialogue one line at a time, jumping to the start of the next line.
principles.quote: Hence, by making dialogue skippable as much as possible, you may just be making a great number of players happy.

principles.principle: Let players listen to dialogue while they keep playing
principles.why: Detailed cutscene performances can't move at the speed players want, and letting dialogue play during gameplay means players don't have to stop and wait.
principles.how: Deliver story or conversation as voiced lines during gameplay instead of pausing play for them.
principles.quote: Or, make it so that people can listen to the dialogue while they play.

summary: The words you use shape your attitude and your actions, so stop broadcasting defeatist thoughts, turn negative feelings into concrete questions about how to improve, and take on challenges fired up.
takeaways: Your words shape your attitude and actions
Avoid voicing defeatist thoughts, especially on social media
Turn negative feelings into questions about improvement
Meet challenges head-on and psych yourself up

principles.principle: Turn negative feelings into concrete questions about how to improve
principles.why: A negative outlook can be a bigger opportunity for change than a positive one if you use it as motivation.
principles.how: When you think 'my work feels pointless,' rewrite it as 'what are some ways I can make it better?' and act on the answer.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating this as forced positivity that denies negative feelings.
principles.quote: If you can use a negative situation as motivation to improve, that might actually be more effective.

principles.principle: Stop voicing defeatist thoughts aloud or on social media
principles.why: Each time you think, say or post a negative idea it becomes a little more true, because your thoughts and words set your attitude toward life.
principles.how: Catch yourself before saying or posting lines like 'there's barely any point in working,' and reframe them or drop them.
principles.anti_pattern: Repeating negative ideas out loud or on social media.
principles.quote: What I mean to say is, your thoughts and words establish your attitude toward life!

principles.principle: Psych yourself up and act head-on when facing a challenge
principles.why: The words you speak tend to set the course of your actions, and those who act are the ones who win.
principles.how: Before a hard task, tell yourself 'Do it! Come on! Go!' and start immediately.
principles.quote: To tie it back to the power of suggestion, those who act are the ones who win.

summary: Always give stuck players a way forward, such as changing difficulty at any time or skipping after repeated failure, because once a player gives up, your challenge is worth nothing.
takeaways: Never let players hit an unbeatable wall
Let difficulty change anytime without restarting
Offer easier modes or skips after repeated failure
Help players without humiliating them
Hardcore design is valid but not for everyone

principles.principle: Let players change difficulty at any time without restarting
principles.why: Games that force a restart because difficulty can't be adjusted have a fundamental design flaw, since once players give up, the challenge is worthless.
principles.how: Make the difficulty setting available mid-playthrough and keep all progress when it changes.
principles.anti_pattern: Locking difficulty at the start so a stuck player has to start over.
principles.quote: Simply letting them change difficulties whenever they want should make a big difference.

principles.principle: Offer stuck players an easier mode or a skip after repeated failures
principles.why: In action games you can't win just by getting stronger, and everyone has a breaking point, so a slightly humiliating offer beats being unable to finish.
principles.how: After several failures in one spot, offer to lower the difficulty or skip the stage as if cleared, worded so it doesn't humiliate the player.
principles.anti_pattern: An impossible difficulty spike at the end of a long game.
principles.example: Some games recommend lowering the difficulty after repeated failure; others let you skip difficult stages.
principles.quote: Even if you diminish the very gameplay itself, that's still better than not being able to beat it.

principles.principle: Choose hardcore difficulty deliberately, knowing not every player wants it
principles.why: Some pleasures only come from intense, unforgiving battles, and hardcore games can be smash hits, but it's best to assume not all players will go for that.
principles.how: If you go hardcore, make it an explicit design goal; otherwise default to kindness, as Kirby's Dream Land did for beginners.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land was tailored to beginners from its inception.
principles.quote: However, it's best to assume that not all players will go for that in every game.

summary: If gameplay depends on telling colors apart, check it through a color-blindness filter and separate similar hues by brightness, and check your art in black and white so backgrounds never outshine the foreground.
takeaways: Never rely solely on color for gameplay distinctions
Check visuals with a color-blindness filter
Separate similar hues with strong brightness differences
Check art in black and white for value balance
Backgrounds shouldn't outshine the foreground

principles.principle: Check color-coded elements with a color-blindness filter; separate them by brightness
principles.why: If a game relies solely on color, color-blind players can't play it, and certain colors tend to look alike across the different types of color blindness.
principles.how: Preview pieces, power-ups and interactive objects through a color-blindness filter (Photoshop includes one), and give similar hues very different brightness without losing them against the background.
principles.anti_pattern: Building gameplay on color differences alone.
principles.example: Meteos: the blocks were checked under a protanopia filter and given significant brightness differences.
principles.quote: If your game is primarily built around color, solely relying on that will make it so that players with color blindness won't be able to play.

principles.principle: Check art in black and white so backgrounds don't outshine the foreground
principles.why: Grayscale makes it obvious which parts are light or dark and what stands out, which fixes prominence problems before they truly begin.
principles.how: Regularly desaturate background art and full screenshots and tone down any background area that draws the eye more than the foreground; flip artwork to spot inconsistencies too.
principles.anti_pattern: Backgrounds that are more prominent than the foreground.
principles.quote: Background art shouldn't be more prominent than the foreground, for example, and this method can fix those problems before they truly begin.

summary: On powerful hardware, judge visuals by the final composited frame (post-processing, blended hues, reflections) rather than by individually polished models, and consider giving post-processing its own specialist.
takeaways: On modern hardware, final output matters more than ever
Post-processing in the framebuffer drives graphical quality
Judge how everything comes together, not individual models
Teams will want dedicated post-processing specialists

principles.principle: Judge visuals by the final composited frame, not individual assets
principles.why: On powerful hardware, post-processing blends the scene together, so it's no longer enough to make polygonal characters look good on their own.
principles.how: Review art with all post-processing enabled, blend hues across the scene, add subtle touches like water reflections, and step back from minor details regularly.
principles.anti_pattern: Polishing individual models while ignoring the whole frame.
principles.example: The same stage in Melee shows a distinct color per object; in Ultimate the hues blend and water reflections improve the final output.
principles.quote: Put simply, it's no longer enough to just focus on making your polygonal characters look good— what matters now is how everything comes together.

principles.principle: Give post-processing and final output a dedicated specialist
principles.why: Sakurai expects experts who oversee post-processing to become the norm and greatly raise the overall quality of in-game visuals.
principles.how: On high-end projects, assign one person to own post-processing and sign off on the final rendered image.
principles.quote: I imagine any team would want to have such a specialist on board.

summary: Keep your reference library of games, consoles, controllers and cables organized and quick to reach, because for a developer old games remain working tools.
takeaways: Keep reference games and hardware organized and accessible
One switchable cabinet gives quick access to many consoles
Label every cable and adapter
Old games stay useful as work reference and footage

principles.principle: Keep reference games and hardware set up for instant access
principles.why: Old games still come in handy for his work, such as footage for the channel, and keeping many systems in one place makes them quick and convenient to use.
principles.how: House consoles together behind a video selector, with switchable power and good ventilation, so you can boot any system in moments.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting the collection go unorganized, which only gets worse over time.
principles.example: Sakurai's custom six-door game cabinet with a selector, used in both his office and his living room.
principles.quote: Especially considering that these old games still come in handy for my line of work.

principles.principle: Give artists physical reference models of the characters they build
principles.why: For Smash Bros. Ultimate, Sakurai bought fighter models for the artists to use as reference material and kept them out on display.
principles.how: Buy figures or models of the characters being modeled and keep them where artists can see them.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: fighter models on display, including Pyra/Mythra figures.
principles.quote: When working on Smash Bros. Ultimate, I bought models of the fighters for the artists to use as reference material

principles.principle: Label every cable, adapter and input in your setup
principles.why: With many consoles hooked up, cables get tangled, and labels let him tell what is plugged into the selector and which adapter goes to what.
principles.how: Label every cable, adapter and selector input with a label printer, and route the cables together down one channel.
principles.example: Tepra labels on the selector wiring and adapters.
principles.quote: This way, I can tell what's plugged into the selector and which adapter goes to what.

summary: Add developer-mode tools that make chosen parts of a model translucent or invisible, and that toggle each display element on or off, so animations and screens can be checked without obstruction.
takeaways: Add dev-mode transparency for selected model parts
Transparency reveals poses hidden by capes and clothes
Per-element display toggles are a must-have
Transparency was quick to implement and widely useful

principles.principle: Build a dev-mode option to make chosen model parts translucent or hidden
principles.why: Capes and clothes hide poses, earlier workarounds like scaling or removing the cape were clumsier, and the feature didn't take long to implement.
principles.how: Let developers select the whole model or individual parts and set them translucent or invisible while reviewing animations, including for checks outside the team.
principles.anti_pattern: Scaling or deleting model parts just to inspect an animation.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's caped fighters; a 3D fighting game developer whose tools could disable clothes and swaying objects.
principles.quote: While this mode is purely for developer use, I highly recommend adding transparency features if possible.

principles.principle: Let developers toggle each display element on or off
principles.why: Sakurai calls per-element display toggles another must-have, and the team used them frequently.
principles.how: Add a debug toggle for each display element so anyone can isolate exactly what they are checking.
principles.quote: This is another must-have!

summary: When balancing, keep characters distinctive by amplifying their shortcomings to offset their strengths, not by sanding their strengths down, because average is mediocre.
takeaways: Average and mediocre are the same thing
Offset strengths by amplifying weaknesses, not cutting advantages
Distinct sides create richer push-and-pull than mirrors
Ultimate's 87 fighters ranged 47.18%–51.43% win rate

principles.principle: Offset strong traits by amplifying weaknesses, not by cutting strengths
principles.why: Balancing purely on strength patches shortcomings and trims advantages until fighters are average, and average isn't fun.
principles.how: When a character overperforms, first exaggerate its weaknesses, and reject proposals that sand away its signature strengths.
principles.anti_pattern: Trimming advantages and patching weaknesses until everyone is average.
principles.example: Smash Bros. tuning team proposals steered to keep fighters unique.
principles.quote: Hence, I advise our team to keep fighters unique by amplifying shortcomings to offset advantages.

principles.principle: Pit distinct sides against each other for richer push and pull
principles.why: Mirror matches like Mario vs. Mario remove balance issues but limit push and pull, while distinct sides create far more variety in strategy.
principles.how: Give each character clear strengths and weaknesses so every matchup calls for different choices.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on identical sides to avoid balance problems.
principles.example: Mario vs. Mario.
principles.quote: Push and pull will still exist if both sides are identical, but there's a limit to how much.

principles.principle: Validate balance with real win-rate data, but trust how characters feel
principles.why: Smash Bros. Ultimate's global online data put all 87 fighters between 47.18% and 51.43%, showing unique fighters can still be balanced, but feel is the true metric.
principles.how: Collect win rates from real matches to confirm every character has a shot, then make final calls based on how each character feels.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's online win rates: highest 51.43%, lowest 47.18%.
principles.quote: I'm not saying that win rates are everything, as the true metric is how each fighter feels

summary: Choose deliberately where your encounters fall between authored, mandatory strategies and free-form approaches, based on your own game's systems rather than copying another game's answer.
takeaways: Authored boss strategies feel like tutorials but show care
Free-form strategies give freedom but less push and pull
Choose the strategic experience your game needs
Derive balance from your systems, not a reference game
games: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

principles.principle: Decide deliberately between authored and free-form encounter strategies
principles.why: Mandatory strategies show crafted thought but feel like tutorials, while free-form ones give freedom but can feel flavorless and create less push and pull; both are valid.
principles.how: For each boss, decide up front whether it has one authored solution, an ideal strategy found by trial and error, or many viable weapon choices.
principles.example: Nintendo bosses where you hit the eye and slash the stunned foe, compared with Castlevania's any-weapon freedom.
principles.quote: Neither answer is more correct than the other, but you'll need to hone in on which experience you want.

principles.principle: Derive strategic balance from your own systems, not a reference game
principles.why: Copying another game's approach ignores your own systems, so learn what there is to learn, then find the balance that fits your game.
principles.how: When studying a reference game's boss design, list its lessons, then rebuild the strategy space from your own mechanics.
principles.anti_pattern: Copying another game's strategy design wholesale.
principles.example: Breath of the Wild feels less mandatory, perhaps because its developers rethought traditional Zelda conventions.
principles.quote: Don't simply reference another game and craft your design based on that— learn what there is to learn, then find the balance that's right for your game's systems.

summary: Rely on dedicated play testers, and on online match data where you have it, to tune balance, while the director steps in mainly to protect each character's individuality.
takeaways: Dedicated play testers know the in-development game best
Directors tuning everything alone barely finish
Use online match and tournament data as reference
Intervene mainly to protect character individuality
games: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Delegate balance analysis to dedicated play testers and trust them
principles.why: Testers battle each other day in and day out and are more attuned to balance than the director, and Sakurai setting every parameter himself through Melee took all he had.
principles.how: Staff full-time play testers, feed their opinions into tuning of every parameter, and use online and tournament results when available.
principles.anti_pattern: A director setting every parameter alone on top of directing.
principles.example: Brawl had only four testers; Ultimate had a much larger, more skilled team plus online data.
principles.quote: However, the play testing team is far more attuned to that than I am, and they battle each other day in and day out, so I trust their analysis.

principles.principle: As director, intervene on balance mainly to protect character individuality
principles.why: Sakurai wants each fighter to be highly unique and player opinions to be divided, and he accepts some unfairness in isolated parts for the sake of individuality.
principles.how: Play the build yourself regularly (he plays 30 minutes of multiplayer at lunch) and step in when a proposed change erodes a character's distinctiveness.
principles.quote: When I do end up saying something, it's most often because a fighter's individuality is being threatened.

principles.principle: Judge balance beyond top-tournament usage, including multiplayer matches
principles.why: A wide spread of fighters at top tournaments is good, but some fighters are naturally better tuned for multiplayer matches.
principles.how: Check how characters perform in multiplayer matches as well as in tournament usage before deciding they need changes.
principles.anti_pattern: Judging fairness from one part of the game in isolation.
principles.quote: I'm glad that top tournament players use a wide range of fighters, but that's not the only thing we look at.

summary: Build CPU opponents from data on reach, timing and the opponent's state, give them human-like reaction limits, and tune them to be fun (aggressive and beatable) rather than flawless.
takeaways: CPUs decide from data: reach, timing, opponent state
Give CPUs human-like reaction delays
Contradictory AI logic causes misbehavior
Tune top CPUs for aggressive fun, not perfect defense

principles.principle: Give CPU players human-like reaction delays
principles.why: CPUs that react faster than a human can feel extremely unfair, and players already tend to suspect computers of cheating.
principles.how: Add a reflex delay before CPUs respond, and let status effects like reversed controls briefly confuse them before they adapt.
principles.anti_pattern: Superhuman reaction speed.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate CPUs have a 'reflex' and get somewhat confused by reversed controls.
principles.quote: if they react faster than a human can, it can feel extremely unfair to players.

principles.principle: Drive action-game AI with precomputed reach, timing and opponent data
principles.why: The computer has no eyes, so it has to decide from data about its own attack and movement ranges, the opponent's attacks, and positioning and status.
principles.how: Convert each character's attack ranges, movement range and attack timing into data the AI can query, and give it the opponent's attack data, position and status.
principles.quote: The computer doesn't have eyes, so it uses information from various categories.

principles.principle: Test layered AI behavior modes for contradictions
principles.why: Switching logic (angry at low HP, keep optimal distance, go easy when winning) can contradict itself, and contradictions grow as mechanics and criteria multiply.
principles.how: List the conditions each behavior mode responds to, and test the cases where two modes would choose opposite actions.
principles.anti_pattern: Piling on behavior criteria without checking for conflicts.
principles.quote: As such, when contradictions arise in the differing logic types, the computer player may not act properly.

principles.principle: Tune top-level CPUs for aggressive offense, not perfect defense
principles.why: Players who choose high CPU levels want strong opponents, and waiting, machine-like reflexes or perfect shields would make CPUs invincible but no fun.
principles.how: Bias high-difficulty AI toward attacking and winning, accept weaker defense and evasion, and cap perfect shields and dodges.
principles.anti_pattern: CPUs that always perfect-shield or dodge every attack.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate CPUs were tuned more aggressively than in past titles.
principles.quote: In the end, it's important to remember that our goal is to make things as fun as possible.
